title: ‘To Be Ordinary’ Review: A Compassionate, Even-Handed Taiwanese Family Melodrama
description: A high-speed traffic accident leaves a college student in a wheelchair for life, but that’s merely the starting point of the narrative in “To Be Or
body:
A high-speed traffic accident leaves a college student in a wheelchair for life, but that’s merely the starting point of the narrative in “To Be Ordinary,” a sensitive, slowly enveloping film with scant interest in disability-drama cliché — instead offering an expansive portrait of how the young man’s entire family is affected by his accident over the course of more than a decade. Spanning marital strife, economic upheaval, coming-of-age pains and moral crisis, Taiwanese writer-director Lee Yun Chan‘s fourth feature — her first since 2010’s “Dancing Without You” — has a lot of story to wrangle, but does so with a mostly delicate, empathetic touch, with a script that treats all individuals in this unhappy scenario with equal care and interest. 
	

	Since her last film, Lee has done mostly small-screen work — directing, among other things, the 2022 Disney+ series “Women in Taipei” — and if a certain televisual strain of melodrama occasional creeps into “To Be Ordinary,” the film’s sturdy formal restraint and expansive story scope should still serve it well in cinemas. Following its premiere as the only Taiwanese production in Busan’s main competition, the film will play at the Tokyo Film Festival later this month, opening theatrically in Taiwan in mid-November. Further festival play is likely, particularly in Asian-focused programs, and the film is accessible and moving enough for limited global distribution, though specialist streaming platforms may be its best bet.


	Lee, who co-wrote the screenplay with “Women in Taipei” scribe Ginger Wang, wastes little time setting the story into motion, opening on a lovely, gliding nighttime tracking shot of 22-year-old Yu-jie (Junior Hsieh) on his moped, cruising the rain-slicked roads of suburban Taipei, as the grandiose strings of Cicada’s score conjure a false feeling of serenity. DP Ming Lee’s camera will certainly never be this free again; the reverie stops short when, at an intersection, Yu-jie is struck by a car, driven by the wealthy, elderly Mr Ma (Hsiu Shen Liang), who’s immediately beset with irremediable guilt.
	

	Yu-jie survives the accident but soon learns, in hospital, that he’ll never walk again; a college student who has already started his own web design business, he accepts the bad news with remarkable stoicism, quickly adapting to life in a wheelchair and seeking ways to live the most normal, productive life possible — which includes a budding relationship with young hospital physiotherapist Yi-Han (Phoebe Chu). 

	If anything, the rest of his family has a harder time adjusting. His mother (Chang Shih Ying) and father (Weber Yang) were already at a fraught point in their marriage, and their son’s plight only drives them further apart, the situation exacerbated by Dad’s longtime unemployment. Meanwhile, Yu-jie’s younger sister Yu-ching (Pin Hsuan Chen), already facing the hormonal turmoil of early adolescence, feels sidelined by the tragedy — pressured to look after herself while, as her mother puts it, “there’s enough going on at home” — and begins to lash out.

	At a pragmatic level, the family is aided by Mr Ma’s crushing conscience: In addition to the required legal settlement, he transfers ownership of his entire house to Yu-jie, and continues to contribute generously toward his medical bills and living expenses. But such generosity can itself become a burden of sorts to the benefactor, particularly as Mr Ma retreats into old age and ill health; avoiding drawing its characters along victims-and-villains lines, “To Be Ordinary” reserves compassion for all in this wretched turn of events, which gives it welcome dramatic complexity and maturity, particularly as the story spans 11 years of evolving consequences.

	Thoughtful, closely-knit ensemble playing keeps the family dynamic believable even when the script takes a few convenient short cuts: Chen is especially affecting and volatile as a young woman growing up both as a kind of afterthought, and as a support system to her flailing parents. Lee directs proceedings with a handsome sobriety that befits the material, though between the persistently overcast visuals and the solemnly emotive writing, “To Be Ordinary” could stand an occasional injection of tonal surprise — an acknowledgement of the absurdity, hilarity or small domestic joys that sometimes disrupt hard times. Still, the film is never glib or unconsidered. There’s unassuming beauty in its even-handed, fair-minded worldview, and the space it gives its characters to reckon with sorrow, and find their own way out of it.

schema.headline: ‘To Be Ordinary’ Review: A Compassionate, Even-Handed Taiwanese Family Melodrama

title: Sylvester Stallone Has ‘Millions of Regrets’ About Doing His Own Stunts: ‘I’m An Idiot for Doing That’
description: Sylvester Stallone is opening up about how decades of daredevilry have affected him—and why he considers himself an “idiot” for continuing to do hi
body:
Sylvester Stallone is opening up about how decades of daredevilry have affected him—and why he considers himself an “idiot” for continuing to do his own stunts year after year.

	In a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the “Rocky” actor said he has “millions, millions of regrets” about his action career. “I could literally spend a half hour talking about injuries, the amount, not even like one, I’m talking about 30 hours, 30 minutes of just individual ones, because it becomes compounded. I have been injured many, many times, but after ‘Expendables,’ I ended up with nine back operations, three neck fusions. Both shoulders ripped out, eye, you know, all kinds of lens put … it’s been brutal,” he said, adding that he’s never been “quite the same” since the surgeries.
	

	Stallone starred in — and also directed — the action thriller “The Expendables” in 2010 alongside Jason Statham, Mickey Rourke and more. While filming a scene where Stallone got tackled by WWE legend Steve Austin, the stunt went wrong and left Stallone with dislocated shoulders and a fractured neck that required more than seven back surgeries. The “Rambo” actor needed a metal plate inserted into his neck and spinal fusions.


	Stallone’s moral of the story is to “let other people do their job.” “Don’t be a stage hawk, or whatever you call it, a showboat. I know a lot of people are thinking about doing stunts … don’t. Don’t. Let the pro do it,” Stallone said. “You cannot beat gravity; when you hit the ground, you lose, and it’s going to come back.”

	He continued, “I mean, just ask every football player in the world. So yeah, and people go, ‘Aren’t you proud of them?’ No. I think I’m an idiot for doing that. I’m proud that I broke myself in pieces. Like, duh, no.”
	

	The actor shared a similar piece of advice ahead of the release of his memoir, “The Steps,” last month; Stallone told The New York Times that treating his body in the “masochistic” ways he did came “at a terrible price.” “If I could do it over again, I would say, ‘Let someone else carry the banner and don’t do your own stunts.”

schema.headline: Sylvester Stallone Has ‘Millions of Regrets’ About Doing His Own Stunts: ‘I’m An Idiot for Doing That’

title: Academy CEO Bill Kramer to Head to Tokyo for Leadership Award and Onstage Summit With Toho Boss Matsuoka Hiro
description: Academy CEO Bill Kramer is set to make his first trip to Asia later this month. He will collect a leadership award at the Tokyo International Film
body:
Academy CEO Bill Kramer is set to make his first trip to Asia later this month. He will collect a leadership award at the Tokyo International Film Festival and also sit down with Toho president and CEO Matsuoka Hiro for a public conversation.

	The festival’s 39th edition runs Oct. 26–Nov. 4 and has built a program titled Academy in Tokyo around the visit. Two colleagues will join Kramer in the Japanese capital: Academy president Lynette Howell Taylor and Meredith Shea, the organization’s chief membership, impact and industry officer.
	

	The three executives will share a stage on Oct. 28 at Tokyo Midtown Hibiya Hall for a 90-minute panel moderated by TIFF festival director Hisamatsu Takeo. They will take the audience behind the curtain of the Oscars and outline the Academy’s international initiatives and membership programs. The conversation will also turn to how the organization views international cinema today and where it is heading.


	Once the panel wraps, Kramer will receive TIFF’s Global Cinema Leadership Special Award. The festival said the honor recognizes his contribution to the growth of the worldwide film business and to film culture. Later that day, the Academy will hold a private reception for its members from across the globe.

	Kramer returns to the same venue on Oct. 29 to sit down with Matsuoka. Their session will look at the state of the global film landscape and the outlook for theatrical and streaming distribution, along with ways to deepen cross-border partnerships. Both public events are free, though advance reservations are required. Booking details have yet to be released.
	

	Kramer took the Academy’s top job in 2022. Before that, he ran the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures as its director and president. The museum opened its doors in September 2021. As CEO, Kramer has pushed to broaden the Academy’s 11,000-strong membership and give it a more international makeup. He runs the organization’s global operations, from the Oscars and the Academy Foundation to the $500 million Academy100 campaign.

	Howell Taylor is in her second term as president. She is an Oscar-nominated producer whose credits include “A Star Is Born,” “The Accountant,” “Captain Fantastic” and “Blue Valentine.” She joined the Academy’s Producers Branch in 2014. She also co-produced the 92nd Oscars telecast in 2020, which earned her an Emmy nomination.

	Shea is the first person to hold her post. Her remit covers membership, awards administration and talent development. It also includes the Academy’s outreach to film festivals and international territories.

	Matsuoka has steered Toho’s expansion overseas, including its acquisitions of Gkids and Anime Limited. He also oversaw the production of Oscar winner “Godzilla Minus One.” In 2025, Toho posted its best-ever results at the Japanese box office. Matsuoka also sits on the board of trustees of the Academy Museum.

	TIFFCOM, the content market that runs alongside the festival, takes place Oct. 28–30.

schema.headline: Academy CEO Bill Kramer to Head to Tokyo for Leadership Award and Onstage Summit With Toho Boss Matsuoka Hiro

title: ‘Abbott Elementary’ Star William Stanford Davis Sets Memoir ‘Don’t Mess With the Fat Kid’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: William Stanford Davis, who stars in “Abbott Elementary” as the janitor Mr. Johnson, is publishing a memoir titled “Don’t Mess With the Fat Kid” vi
body:
William Stanford Davis, who stars in “Abbott Elementary” as the janitor Mr. Johnson, is publishing a memoir titled “Don’t Mess With the Fat Kid” via BenBella Books.

	“Don’t Mess With the Fat Kid” will dive into Davis’ life and career — including struggles such as addiction and rejection — and the experience of nabbing his breakout role at age 70. Per the official description, Davis’ story is written in three parts: “The first will chronicle Davis’ childhood in the 1960s in the Ville, a predominantly Black neighborhood in St. Louis. The second will follow him as a young man, fresh off the bus in ‘country-ass’ Jefferson City in the early 1970s. The final section will chronicle Davis’ journey, well into his forties, from addict to working actor, and the years of perseverance, rejection and hard-earned experience that ultimately led to the biggest role of his career.”
	

	“Don’t Mess With the Fat Kid” was sold to BenBella Books editor and CEO Glen Yeffeth by Miles Blim at Aevitas Creative Management in association with Innovative Artists. It will be released in hardcover, e-book, and audiobook formats.


	Besides “Abbott Elementary,” Davis’ credits include the Wanda Sykes film “Undercard,” Apple TV’s “Swagger,” HBO’s “Curb Your Enthusiasm,” Showtime’s “Ray Donovan” and ABC’s “Lincoln Heights.” 

	“I’ve wanted to write this memoir for a long time, to honor the road I’ve taken to get here and to connect with folks who are still on their way,” Davis said in a statement. “People know me as Mr. Johnson from ‘Abbott Elementary,’ and while that’s the biggest role of my career so far, it’s not the whole story. I’m excited to finally share the full story: the struggles, the setbacks, the second chances and the perseverance it took to keep going and get to where I am today. It took me a long time to get here, and the beautiful thing is, I’m just getting started.”

schema.headline: ‘Abbott Elementary’ Star William Stanford Davis Sets Memoir ‘Don’t Mess With the Fat Kid’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Lanterns’ Season 2 Won’t Be Greenlit Until the Writers’ Room ‘Comes Up With a Worthy Successor to a Great First Season’
description: While HBO’s “Lanterns” hasn’t yet scored a second season renewal, one could be on the way depending on how things go in the writers’ room, accordin
body:
While HBO’s “Lanterns” hasn’t yet scored a second season renewal, one could be on the way depending on how things go in the writers’ room, according to DC Studios co-chief Peter Safran. 

	While he didn’t confirm an exact date fans can expect an announcement to come on, Safran did note that news on whether “Lanterns” will get a second season should arrive “before the end of the year” in a recent interview with Collider. Safran also noted that Season 2 would need to be up to par with Season 1, which enjoyed a massively successful premiere and run. “If we’re able to come up with what we believe to be a worthy successor to a beloved and great first season, that’s what’s going to dictate whether there’s a second season,” he said.
	

	Safran added that the most rewarding part of Season 1’s success has been seeing the “Green Lantern” property back in the cultural conversation. (“Lanterns” was adapted from DC Comics’ “Green Lantern” franchise, which follows an intergalactic police force.)


	The eight-episode show’s season finale aired on Oct. 4, and wrapped up the central mystery of who killed Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) and revealed the identity of the second Manhunter, plus how John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) becomes Earth’s sole Green Lantern in DC Studios’ forthcoming “Superman” sequel, “Man of Tomorrow.”

	Before the finale, Variety reported that the show’s seventh episode reached 7 million viewers in the U.S. in its first three days of availability. Previous episodes had averaged over 12 million viewers per episode in the U.S. to date and nearly 19 million when factoring in international viewing.

schema.headline: ‘Lanterns’ Season 2 Won’t Be Greenlit Until the Writers’ Room ‘Comes Up With a Worthy Successor to a Great First Season’

title: ‘Beach Fictions’ Review: Utterly Beguiling, Time-Tweaking Korean Romance Shows What a Day a Difference Makes
description: Fatalism, self-determination and imagination all gently wrestle for control of the narrative(s) in “Beach Fictions,” an enchanting and subtly profo
body:
Fatalism, self-determination and imagination all gently wrestle for control of the narrative(s) in “Beach Fictions,” an enchanting and subtly profound diptych that follows one young woman through two diverging versions of the same day — saying much in the process about the voices, inner and otherwise, that we grant most control in our lives, for better or worse. Though its structuring principle of a single day playing out twice consecutively to differing effect (as opposed to braiding its alternate timelines like “Sliding Doors” or “Blind Chance”) explicitly recalls Hong Sangsoo’s “Right Now, Wrong Then,” this chicly poised debut feature by fellow South Korean Lim Hayeon has a style, tone and outlook of its own, maintained with impressive control over a surprisingly breezy-feeling 145 minutes.
	

	One of the real discoveries in this year’s main competition at the Busan Film Festival, “Beach Fictions” should have little difficulty charming other programmers on the international fest circuit following its world premiere — while only its running time, manageable but unexpectedly robust for a film this light on its feet, presents an obstacle to global arthouse distribution, or at least specialist streaming exposure. Either way, this graduation project (produced by the  Korean Academy of Film Arts) announces its writer-director-editor as one to watch, should her future films match this one’s warmth and formal elegance; in only her second big-screen outing after years of TV work, winsome lead Hansol Park also feels like a breakout talent.


	“Beach Fictions” pulls you in from its first iridescent frame, as Sinuk Park’s camera glides serenely from a bejeweled nighttime view of Incheon through the chattery hubbub of a mood-lit restaurant where Tae-ju (Park), seen only from behind, is dining with friends, their conversation seemingly more animated than hers. Even without the detached voiceover — which turns out to belong to perceptive novelist Ewha (Sujeong Ye), describing the superficial response of Tae-ju’s friends to an anecdote she shares — we’d sense her loneliness amid company. Later, when her friends abandon her at the table to smoke outside, she’s crushed to find them gossiping about her; shortly afterwards, in a never-rains-but-pours development, she breaks up with her casual boyfriend Hyun-jin after he expresses scant interest in taking the relationship further.
	

	With her social life in tatters and a world of her anxieties realized, Tae-ju rashly skips town, heading for the tranquil coastal guesthouse of another friend. On the train there, she encounters Ewha, whom we’ve already seen observing her from afar at the restaurant, and confides in the kindly, silver-haired older woman — who says Tae-ju resembles the protagonist of the novel she’s currently writing. But is she the  writer’s inspiration or her creation, an incomplete fiction who has somehow taken on an agency of her own? From here on out, the authorship of Tae-ju’s life is ambiguous, as well as constantly in flux, buffeted by the whims and suggestions of others, as well as by her own impulses.

	In the sleepy beach town, she meets and is immediately entranced by charismatic street magician Manhyuk (Kim Wookyum, delightful), only to later be warned off him by her hostess, who claims he’s a local lothario and sometime sex worker. A day in his company turns sour but when, in the film’s deftly shuffled second half, she meets him in slightly different circumstances, and the day’s events take on a different chain of connections, the potential romantic outcome differs too. 

	Her nascent relationship with Manhyuk is the chief variable of Tae-ju’s two stories, but other, slighter factors push it this way and that: a water-damaged phone in need of repair; a hangout with fellow guesthouse patrons that echoes or corrects her earlier social fallout; and a consultation with a psychic, recommended by Ehwa, whose counsel also shifts her fate. The contrasts between the two tales are never drastic; the gradations are sometimes as fine as those between warm and cool melancholy. The camerawork is consistently, richly sun-flooded, but some compositions isolate Tae-ju more than others; Wonhong Lee’s delicate jazz piano score can similarly tilt a situation from cozy to nervy.

	But both gently lolloping narratives hold the attention, in large part thanks to Park’s deeply sympathetic performance as Hae-ju, simultaneously played as a fragile, will-o’-the-wisp go-alonger — or perhaps just an author’s as-yet-unformed blank canvas — and a wounded flesh-and-blood human now guarding her emotions more carefully. It’s a canny turn completely in synch with Lim’s complex, metatextual script, which brims with ideas about the fictional construction process, as well the real-life bind felt by vulnerable young women expected to bend to others’ desires and expectations. Is life itself not just a series of drafts and redrafts, with notes we either learn from or don’t, our characters never not in progress? Wry and wise and happy-sad, “Beach Fictions” crosses nothing out, alive to all possibilities.

schema.headline: ‘Beach Fictions’ Review: Utterly Beguiling, Time-Tweaking Korean Romance Shows What a Day a Difference Makes

title: ‘The Lowdown’ Creator Sterlin Harjo on the Films That Inspired Season 2, and What Convinced Tommy Lee Jones to Join the Show
description: As “The Lowdown” Season 2 opens, citizen journalist (or “truthstorian”) Lee Raybon (Ethan Hawke) is in a completely uncomfortable position: success
body:
As “The Lowdown” Season 2 opens, citizen journalist (or “truthstorian”) Lee Raybon (Ethan Hawke) is in a completely uncomfortable position: success. He’s about accept a local media award for a piece he wrote about the death of Dale Washberg (as detailed in Season 1 of the series), but isn’t happy about it.

	Rather than accept his acclaim, a boozy Lee gets on stage and immediately tears into the crowd for being sellouts. It doesn’t go well. Series creator Sterlin Harjo admits to Variety that Lee’s inability to deal with a bit of acclaim comes directly from his own experience after the launch of his previous FX series, “Reservation Dogs.”
	

	“I was living in a studio loft in downtown Tulsa, and all of a sudden I had a TV show,” he says. “I had been a kind of quiet independent filmmaker hoping to get some attention from anyone in this industry with my films. But then, ‘Reservation Dogs’ Season 1 truly changed my whole life. And I didn’t handle it well at first. You don’t know what to do. All of a sudden, there’s articles, and there’s all this stuff and you’re very exposed. It was fun thinking of that as Lee Raybon, because how does he handle the little recognition that he got? I bet he handles it really wrong, and I bet that there is a knee-jerk reaction to reject it.”


	The theme of Season 2, Harjo says, is to figure out how to love yourself — and how that love will extend to everyone else in your life. After that initial shock of his “Reservation Dogs” success, Harjo is getting there. It helps that he has another critically acclaimed series on his hands.
	

	Conceivably, “The Lowdown” could go on forever, given that there’s no shortage of story fodder about the amount of profligacy that exists in the world. After Season 1, “I wasn’t finished telling the story,” he says. “There was more of the corruption that I could tell.”

	As Season 2 premieres on Oct. 14 on FX, Lee is soon recruited by public defender Ginger (Betty Gilpin) to investigate a new mystery: the disappearance of her client inside the Oklahoma prison system.

	This time out, Harjo says he was inspired by the 1972 Lee Marvin/Gene Hackman film “Prime Cut,” 1981’s “Cutter’s Way” and the 1949 noir “The Third Man” to come up with the underlying concept.

	“This idea of a missing man, I was like, how do we amp this up a little bit?” he says. “Well, it’s really hard to go missing in prison. There’s a sign-in sheet. How do you go missing from prison? That was such an intriguing question.”

	Harjo says he, fellow exec producer Duffy Boudreau and Hawke began brainstorming the idea while doing their press tour for Season 1 of “The Lowdown.”

	“That’s when we came up with kind of the bones of the plot,” he says. “Through lots of influences, and also just Oklahoma.”

	Harjo says they also got to know Hawke’s cousin, a public defender in Ft. Worth, who shared stories about her experiences. “And I grew up in a town with a prison, and I saw how that affects a town,” he adds. “You really saw this shift in the town, and not a positive one. Because you have drugs, you have trafficking, you have drug trafficking of guards and prisoners.”

	For inspiration, Harjo also remembers visiting his uncle as a kid in a McAlester, Oklahoma, prison, where he was doing time for repeat alcohol offenses. “The Lowdown” wound up shooting in that very same institution this season.

	But that’s just one half of Season 2. The show’s other bombshell comes at the end of the opening episode: Tommy Lee Jones shows up as Lee’s estranged father.

	“We talked a lot about being a father in Season 1. What’s it like being a son? And how do you forgive your father or a parent?” Harjo says. But just as Lee Sr. neglected his son growing up, Lee Jr. continues to mess things up with his own daughter, Francis (Ryan Kiera Armstrong).
	

	“He’s trying to not make bad decisions [like his father],” Harjo says. “And at the same time, he’s neglecting his daughter, which is a bad decision. And then, his father, who was a bad father, is connecting with his granddaughter.” 

	“The more complicated you can make all that stuff, the better, because you’ve got to fight your way out of it as a writer,” Harjo says. “It was a very painful writing experience, more painful than anything, because I had written myself into so many corners. There was stuff that I was writing, there was episodes being written deep into production. I hope I never have to do that again!”

	After writing the first episode of Season 2, Harjo immediately thought of Jones for the part as Lee’s father. Both he and Jones are both represented by CAA — and once Jones read it, the actor wanted in. Jones had already watched Season 1 — and told Harjo that he specifically loved the bookstore security guards Waylon (Cody Lightning) and Cousin Henry (Jude Barnett), who provide some comic relief.

	“He wanted to be with them, which that told me everything I needed to know,” Harjo says. “If you love the security guards, you love me and the show and the vibe. Because those characters wouldn’t necessarily be on a lot of shows. You would cut that. After the premiere the other day, [Jones] says, ‘Thanks for paying attention to the character Waylon, because most people wouldn’t. It’s characters and storylines like that I think make the show what it is.’”

	Harjo also excitedly notes that Jones started watching “Reservation Dogs” while shooting “The Lowdown.”

	“There was something amazing about every day coming to work and having Tommy Lee Jones describe an episode of the show that I created,” he says. “He’d be talking to Ethan or me about it, and it was nice that he appreciated it so much. ‘Reservation Dogs’ is the type of show that you might think someone like Tommy Lee Jones could miss and not get it, but he’s a sophisticated, really smart artist and he loved it. It was amazing every day.”

	As for the character of Ginger, she’s clearly a love interest for Lee — a tough character who can go toe-to-toe with him, but has a humor to her as well. Once Gilpin came on board, Harjo says she helped redefine who Ginger could be.
	

	“Lee can be a bit wild, and I needed someone to match that energy,” Harjo says. “Betty can do anything, and I already knew that she was great. And then she came, and it was like another level. All of a sudden she’s doing things in the first scene that I’m filming with her, and there’s things happening that I did not write. From that day forward, I’m trying to write toward her voice and what she’s bringing to that character.”

	Harjo says he aimed to make Season 2 “go harder and faster with everything that we have established. It’s kind of like ‘Reservation Dog’ Season 2 as well. I’ve established the world. I feel like people that like the show will come with me. I have a meter of what feels real and what doesn’t, so I always sort of adhere to that. Let’s make ‘Empire Strikes Back,’ where it’s great and it stands on its own, but you also want more by the end. Gods of TV willing, we’ll be making a Season 3 of this show.”

	The first two episodes of “The Lowdown” Season 2 premiere on FX and Hulu on Oct. 14 at 9 p.m. ET, with remaining episodes airing weekly on Wednesdays

title: Critics Vindicate ‘Artificial’ After Messy Amazon MGM Breakup (and the Studios vs. Talent Wars Around AI Are Just Beginning)
description:
Looks like “Artificial” is the real thing.

body:
Looks like “Artificial” is the real thing.

	Luca Guadagnino’s genre-blending movie about the evils of artificial intelligence (and one of its fathers, Sam Altman) had a triumphant U.K. premiere at the London Film Festival on Sunday. The director, standing beside key cast members Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov, received thunderous applause at Royal Festival Hall.

	The British event followed the world premiere of “Artificial” a week earlier at the New York Film Festival. It was a make-or-break moment for a project plagued by scandal after Amazon MGM punted the film off its summer slate. Worse was what came after: an odious whisper campaign saying the film stank (anonymous sources dismissed it as only worthy of a streaming release, according to a July report). But the Big Apple swallowed the film with rapture.
	

	“So this is a dawn-of-a-new-world story, as well as a backstabbing corporate business story, and also a horror movie, in which AI emerges from the lab as a sinister serpent,” wrote Variety chief critic Owen Gleiberman in his review, calling the movie a “brilliant but playful docudrama, meticulously true to history.”


	Others agree. The title has a 96% Fresh rating on review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes, representing the highest score of Guadagnino’s career across 11 feature film releases. Garfield has been catapulted to the front of the best supporting actor race, thanks to a performance that delivers “a masterclass in diabolical villainy,” according to another review.

	The notices, the standing ovations, the awards buzz — all of it represents a stunning reversal of fortune for Guadagnino after the Amazon debacle in June. It was highly uncommon, in Hollywood terms, for even a tech-owned content studio to kill a project it had cradled since infancy. Neon rescued the movie with a global rights deal shortly after the Amazon rift.
	

	“We believe that ‘Artificial’ will be better served if it were released by a different studio,” the e-commerce giant said at the time. Global press almost unanimously noted that the decision to jettison the movie came only three months after Amazon signed a significant partnership with Altman’s OpenAI (including a $50 billion investment in the company).

	But, per Variety’s sources, the writing is on the wall. Nothing was wrong with “Artificial,” and the response underlines the dubiousness of Amazon’s decision to drop it. 

	“Wasn’t this supposed to be god-awful?” wondered one film executive at a rival studio. The exec didn’t just raise an eyebrow at Amazon MGM, but at other legacy distributors who were in the mix to take the project before Neon won out. “A reaction this strong just shows you, every studio pretending the film wasn’t releasable is just conflicted out by their own investments in AI.”

	In July, New York magazine published a piece citing individuals close to the project as saying it “lacked theater-worthy criteria.” That doesn’t quite track with early audience response. In fact, the critical consensus is that “Artificial” — not Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning,” which debuted last weekend via Sony Pictures — is a worthy spiritual successor to David Fincher’s “The Social Network.” It’s hard to imagine Amazon not being pleased with this response had it kept “Artificial.”

	Interestingly, Amazon’s headaches at the intersection of talent and AI are not exclusive to the Guadagnino movie. At New York Comic Con last weekend, actor Nicolas Cage made waves when he disclosed that he refused to sign a document permitting the studio to use AI in and around his likeness on its now-canceled original series “Spider-Noir.”

	“I am not an AI-friendly actor. I’m not a member of their club. I didn’t sign the waiver,” Cage said. “I’m probably not going to be working with that studio again.” There’s a bit more to this story, insiders close to “Spider-Noir” said. Cage was referring to a form from the show’s producer, Sony Pictures Television, considered “industry standard” on content shoots. The waiver gives the studio permission to create a duplicate of an actor in costume, which aids in VFX work during postproduction. Actors are free to opt out, and the form is said to be in line with SAG-AFTRA guidelines.
	

	But it won’t be the end of talent bristling over the coming AI revolution — at Amazon or elsewhere. One creative team member on an Amazon MGM series tells Variety that AI training is a requirement on the lot these days.

	The source describes a “mandatory and perfunctory meeting” with the company’s AI team, billed as standard workplace education that corporations regularly hold around sexual harassment and fire safety. The AI group spent an hour pitching the creatives on a suite of products it referred to as “tools.” Our source says, however, it became clear that these tools could “eliminate entire jobs” on the production. Amazon MGM declined to comment on the matter.

	More telling, per the source, is that the show’s corporate stewards from Amazon also sat through the training “stone-faced.” While the individual won’t name the execs in attendance, they found it “collectively embarrassing for everyone to be doing this, including on the Amazon side.” A source with direct knowledge of Amazon’s process said such meetings are not mandatory, and humans guide every part of the process related to the tools. 

	And so begins the great sacrifice the major studios are about to make in service of computer-based cost efficiencies and the “move fast and break things” bravado of Silicon Valley. Time will tell if a prompt can make content that’s as buzzy and well positioned as “Artificial.”

schema.headline: Critics Vindicate ‘Artificial’ After Messy Amazon MGM Breakup (and the Studios vs. Talent Wars Around AI Are Just Beginning)

Move over, Chalamet — there’s a new white boy of the year.

In the 2026 edition, that honorific went to Justin Bieber, who beat out fellow nominees Tom Holland, Erling Haaland, Robert Pattinson and Travis Kelce. Bieber made an appearance in the awards special alongside fellow winners Michael B. Jordan, Druski, Coco Gauff, 50 Cent and more.
	

	The Believe That Awards, now live on Edwards’ YouTube channel and social media profiles and presented by PrizePicks, are produced by Edwards through his Three Fifths Media banner alongside Wheelhouse and Portal A. The special is meant to “celebrates standout moments, cultural disruptors and iconic achievements across sports and entertainment, filtered through the unapologetic and uncensored lens of Edwards.”

	“We’re back, and we raised the bar across the board this year,” Edwards said in a statement. “You know me, which means you know we have the same unfiltered, totally unpredictable energy that is always built for and aimed directly at the culture. We brought together the biggest names in the game to chop it up, have fun and celebrate real greatness on our own terms. You’re not getting this vibe anywhere else.”

	“From day one, our mission at Three Fifths Media has been to create content that remains fiercely authentic to Anthony and the community that moves with him,” said Justin Holland, who is Edwards’ business manager and co-founder of Three Fifths Media. “The Believe That Awards sits at the true epicenter of sports, entertainment and culture. title: ‘Full House’ Star Jodie Sweetin Says Dave Coulier is ‘Doing Great’ Following ‘Tough Battle’ with Cancer
description: Jodie Sweetin is giving fans a health update on her “Full House” co-star Dave Coulier, eight months after the actor announced he was in remission f
body:
Jodie Sweetin is giving fans a health update on her “Full House” co-star Dave Coulier, eight months after the actor announced he was in remission from tongue cancer.

	Speaking with People, Sweetin said Coulier is doing “really well,” and she’d just spent a weekend at his house with Andrea Barber, who played Kimmy Gibler on the ABC sitcom. The actress agreed Coulier has had “such a tough battle,” explaining that “sitting around and having coffee with him in the morning meant so much.” The two recently connected at an arts fundraiser in Detroit, which was “so much fun,” she added. “He’s doing great.”
	

	Sweetin also noted their bond has lasted since acting on-screen together more than 30 years ago. “We’re still super close,” she said. “We’re all doing 90s Con in Hartford this coming weekend. Yeah, we’re like obnoxiously annoyingly close… We’re a family.”


	Sweetin played Stephanie Tanner on the beloved sitcom, while Coulier played Joey Gladstone, Danny Tanner’s best friend (though he’s referred to as “Uncle Joey” on the show). “Full House” ran for eight seasons, from 1987 to 1995.

	In Feb., Coulier revealed he was in remission after undergoing treatment for tongue cancer, a diagnosis he had shared in December. He had beaten Stage 3 non-Hodgkin Lymphoma nearly a year before that. “It’s been a roller coaster ride for sure,” Coulier said during an appearance on “Good Morning America.” “I’m in remission with both cancers. And what a journey this has been.”

	Three months later, the actor took to social media to respond to fans who pointed out his changing appearance following both cancers, sharing on Instgram that he hadn’t been able to eat solid food in months and lost 45 pounds.
	

	“Hi everyone, it’s me Dave, and I haven’t posted in quite a while and the last time I did some of you said that I look differently, and I sound differently, and I do,” he began the video. “And what you’re seeing is the side effects of extensive radiation that I went through for carcinoma in my throat… It’s affected my ability to speak, some of you have said that I speak differently. So you’re right on with what you’re seeing and what you’re hearing.”

schema.headline: ‘Full House’ Star Jodie Sweetin Says Dave Coulier is ‘Doing Great’ Following ‘Tough Battle’ with Cancer

'7 Little Johnstons' Star Anna
                          Busted for DUI … Cheesing in Mug Shot
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            "7 Little Johnstons" star Anna Johnston was hauled into jail after being arrested for DUI ... and flashed a big smile for her mug shot.
      
    
            According to a police report obtained by multiple outlets, Anna was arrested in Georgia on Saturday after cops saw her car parked on the side of the highway and investigated. 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The report says Anna was driving her boyfriend, Jeffrey Messervy, and his cousin when she got into an argument with Jeffrey and pulled over. They say Jeffrey told them he was "upset due to Anna driving them around with alcohol in her system."
      
    
            Anna was allegedly slurring her speech when the officer arrived and was asked to take a breathalyzer ... and cops say she blew a 0.139. Police say she reeked of booze and bombed a field sobriety test, so they arrested her for DUI. 
      

                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The day after her DUI bust, Anna was released from the local jail on $1,563 bond.
      
    
            The Sun reports Jeffrey had a warrant out and was also arrested … and he's apparently being held on a $47,350 bond for 13 counts of misdemeanor forgery.
      
    
            Anna left "7 Little Johnstons" after season 16 because of her rocky relationship with her family.

title: Halle Berry's Son Maceo Allowed to Testify in Custody Battle with Olivier Martinez
description:
Halle Berry
                          Son Allowed to Testify in Explosive Custody Battle with Ex
body:
Halle Berry
                          Son Allowed to Testify in Explosive Custody Battle with Ex
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 14, 2026
                            5:48 PM PDT
                                                                            
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Halle Berry's son, Maceo, will be allowed to take the stand in her bitter custody battle with Olivier Martinez, TMZ has learned.
      
    
            According to court docs obtained by TMZ ... the 13-year-old has been permitted to testify, but his testimony will be "limited to the request for the issuance of a restraining order."
      
    
            Olivier's requesting a domestic violence restraining order, claiming Halle attacked their son during an argument while he was playing a virual reality video game.
      

            He alleges Halle jumped on Maceo, put her hands around his neck, and choked him ... Halle denies she hurt their son.
      
    
            Olivier's seeking sole custody of Maceo and is asking the court to make Halle stay away.
      
    
            Halle's been trying to keep the court from allowing their son to testify, arguing that Olivier's been coaching him on what to say.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            TMZ has also obtained Halle's response to Olivier's DVRO request ... she says Maceo has a "personal interest in minimizing his own conduct and shifting responsibility to others," arguing that the court can't necessarily assume his account is reliable.
      
    
            Halle goes on to say that she's been concerned for years that Olivier was getting their son involved in adult arguments, claiming their dynamic has caused her to be the rule enforcer while Olivier gets to be the chill parent.
      
    
            She says this has caused Maceo to view her as the "bad guy" and Olivier as the "good guy" for allowing him to have "greater autonomy."
      
    
            Halle's worried that this dynamic will influence Maceo's testimony to reflect "perceptions developed over time" rather than an accurate account of what happened.
      
    
            But it seems that, for now, the court's siding with Olivier and allowing Maceo to testify. The judge did note that any testimony from the teen will be in a closed courtroom with only the parties, counsel, and court personnel present.

schema.headline: Halle Berry's Son Maceo Allowed to Testify in Custody Battle with Olivier Martinez

title: Lindsay Clancy Holdout Juror Doubles Down, Says Evidence Backed His Vote
description:
Lindsay Clancy Holdout Juror
                          I Had Evidence the Other 11 Jurors Didn't
body:
Lindsay Clancy Holdout Juror
                          I Had Evidence the Other 11 Jurors Didn't Buy!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                October 14, 2026
                
                            1:53 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  October 14, 2026
                                2:37 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            The lone holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial is doubling down on his belief she's guilty ... claiming he had plenty of evidence to back up his position, but he's keeping some of it under wraps.
      
    
            Michael Desronvil sat down with Fox News's Kayleigh McEnany ... insisting he had absolutely no reasonable doubt about Clancy's guilt, despite 11 other jurors believing she wasn't criminally responsible for killing her 3 children.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            And while Desronvil says he had plenty of evidence to support his decision, he's not spilling all the details ... saying he wants to respect the other jurors and let the court process play out.
      

            He does admit things got heated inside the jury room ... which probably isn't surprising, considering he was the only one standing in the way of a unanimous verdict after 38 hours of deliberations.
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported ... Desronvil already pushed back on accusations he ignored reasonable doubt, telling us last month he believed Clancy carefully planned the killings.
      
    
            Other jurors have painted a very different picture ... accusing Desronvil of refusing to budge despite allegedly acknowledging doubts about the case.
      
    
            Clancy's defense maintains she was suffering from postpartum psychosis when her children died ... while prosecutors argued she knew exactly what she was doing.
      
    
            The case remains up in the air after a judge rejected Clancy's attempt to have the murder charges tossed earlier this month.
      
    
            Desronvil's full interview airs Thursday morning on "Fox & Friends."
